g.text: Streams and tables — the two faces of one dataset
9 stream records ↔ 2 table rows · both total 45
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · table a:24 b:21 · total 45
THE STREAM — AN APPEND-ONLY SEQUENCE OF CHANGES
9 records, each one a CHANGE — nothing here is a current value
Every row is a delta. To answer "what is key \"a\" now?" you must read all of them and add up — the stream does not hold an answer, it holds a
history.
What it DOES hold that a table cannot: the order, and every intermediate value that ever existed.
Step 1/4 — the stream: what happened, in order
A stream answers "what happened". Each of the 9 rows is a change, so the current value of anything is a computation rather than a lookup. In
exchange you get something a table throws away: the order, and every value the system ever held.
Streams and tables — the two faces of one dataset
9 stream records ↔ 2 table rows · both total 45
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · table a:24 b:21 · total 45
THE TABLE — ONE ROW PER KEY, CURRENT VALUE
2 rows, answering "what is true now" in one lookup
key "a"
24 (from 5 events: 5 + 3 + 2 + 6 + 8)
key "b"
21 (from 4 events: 7 + 1 + 9 + 4)
9 stream records became 2 table rows. The table is smaller, faster to query — and it has forgotten the order and every intermediate value.
Ask it "was key \"a\" ever 8?" and it cannot answer. The stream can.
Step 2/4 — the table: what is true now
A table answers "what is true now" in a lookup rather than a fold: 9 records collapse to 2 rows. The cost is in the note — the table has forgotten
the order and every intermediate value, so a question about history is unanswerable from it even though no information was deliberately discarded.
Streams and tables — the two faces of one dataset
9 stream records ↔ 2 table rows · both total 45
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · table a:24 b:21 · total 45
ONE DATASET, TWO SHAPES
the totals agree because neither view invented or lost anything
the stream totals
45 over 9 records
the table totals
45 over 2 rows
the stream is
the table's HISTORY — every change that produced it
the table is
the stream's PRESENT — the fold of every change so far
The two totals are equal, and that equality is the duality stated as an arithmetic check rather than as a slogan.
Neither view is primary by nature. The stream is primary by CHOICE, because it is the one you can rebuild the other from.
Step 3/4 — and they are the same data, folded differently
Both totals are 45, which is the duality in its most checkable form: the two views contain the same information, arranged for different questions.
The second note is the design consequence — neither is inherently the source of truth, and the stream earns that role because the derivation only
runs one way cheaply.
Streams and tables — the two faces of one dataset
9 stream records ↔ 2 table rows · both total 45
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · table a:24 b:21 · total 45
THE SAME DUALITY, TWO INDUSTRIES
neither is wrong; each optimised for one of the two questions
a relational database
table-centric: stores the 2 rows, derives history only if you ask for it
an event log (e.g. Kafka)
stream-centric: stores the 9 records, derives the rows on read
a stream processor
sits between them — consumes the stream, maintains the table
what each one gives up
the DB gives up history; the log gives up cheap lookups
A database with an audit log and a Kafka topic with a materialized view are converging on the same thing from opposite ends.
So "should we use a database or an event log?" is usually the wrong question. The real one is which view is the SOURCE and which is DERIVED.
Step 4/4 — so databases and event logs each picked a side
Reading the industry split this way makes the architectural choice concrete. A database stores 2 rows and can give you history only if someone
added an audit table; a log stores 9 records and makes every lookup a fold. The useful question is never which technology — it is which of the two
views you treat as truth.
